A risk remains if a process crashes after a payment goes through but before the result is saved. Render recommends using idempotency keys to prevent duplicate charges or database writes. Shared Filesystems let sandboxes and workflow tasks access the same persistent files, even after the compute that created them shuts down.

Render says the feature is designed for “many agents reading the same repo or dataset, with each one writing its own output.” But handling “concurrent writes to the same file, including locking and conflict resolution, is something we’re still studying,” the company tells The New Stack. [...] Not everything is ready yet. Credential brokering will initially be available only to selected customers, private networking for sandboxes is still in development, and Render has yet to settle how its shared storage will handle simultaneous writes to the same file.

## Sandboxes that resume mid-task

With this launch, Render sandboxes can stay active through a multi-day codebase migration or while an agent tests an entire application.

The bigger difference comes when a sandbox needs to resume work. Vercel limits uninterrupted sessions to 24 hours, and while persistent sandboxes can restart, their running processes start over.

results.title: Render Sandboxes Computer for Every AI Agent: Public Beta Review
results.content:
Every Render sandbox is its own Firecracker microVM: a fully isolated Linux computer with its own filesystem, its own processes, and persistent state. That isolation is the whole point. An AI agent that installs packages, edits files, and runs code needs a machine of its own — not a corner of your application server, and not a shared container where one bad command can touch another user’s data. [...] Three numbers from Render’s launch define the product. First, a sandbox is ready for its first command in under a second, even when traffic arrives in bursts. Second, you can run thousands of sandboxes at once. Third, there is no time limit: a sandbox can run for hours, days, or months. When it goes idle, Render suspends it automatically — by default after 15 minutes with no commands or file transfers — and wakes it on the next command with its files, memory, and running processes intact. You do not pay for compute while it is suspended. [...] ## What It Does in Practice

### 1. Run your agent inside a sandbox

Give your agents tools, files, and processes that persist between sessions. The canonical example is running an agent harness such as Claude Code or Codex inside the sandbox, so the agent has a real machine to work on rather than a stateless function call. Your product creates a sandbox through the SDK, uploads the task, streams the agent’s commands and output, and terminates the sandbox when the work is done. Because state persists across suspend and resume, a long-running task can pause for hours — waiting on a human approval, for instance — and continue without losing its place.

### 2. Spin up a full copy of your app

results.content:
Private networking, so sandboxes can reach the rest of your Render services without going over the public internet.
 More regions beyond Oregon.
 SSH access and public URLs, so you can work inside a running sandbox and open the app an agent started from your browser.
 CPU and memory bursting, so a sandbox can temporarily use more resources for heavy work without moving to a larger size.
 Shared Filesystems are also coming soon. A Shared Filesystem gives your sandboxes and workflow tasks the same persistent files, so parallel agents can read shared inputs, write their own outputs, and build on each other's work. Files stay put after the compute that used them shuts down. Request early access. [...] ## Scale reliably from one sandbox to thousands

While sandboxes are new to Render, reliably spinning up isolated environments on demand is not. Render already does this for every build, more than one million times a day.

Drawing on that experience, we built Render Sandboxes to hold up whether you run one sandbox or thousands. Each one is typically ready for its first command in under one second; even faster when it’s restored from a snapshot. Expect startup time to improve through the beta.

## Your sandboxes run next to the rest of your app [...] Each sandbox starts from an image: Render’s default, or a custom image that already includes your agent harness, dependencies, and configuration. From there, two types of snapshots can capture its progress:

1. A filesystem snapshot saves files and installed tools. Use it to skip setup on new sandboxes, or to carry an agent’s notes from one session to the next.
2. A runtime snapshot (the default) also saves memory and running processes, so your agent picks up mid-task instead of reloading its state from disk. This can make startup 3x to 10x faster.

# Render launches Render Sandboxes public beta

news.ycombinator.com5 min read

Render has launched Render Sandboxes in public beta, providing isolated Linux environments using Firecracker microVMs designed for AI agents to run code and install dependencies securely. The sandboxes support indefinite execution, automatic suspension when idle, filesystem and runtime snapshots for faster startup, and credential brokering to prevent API key leaks.Open article →
